job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Karl Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house near Ashby station with two other guys, one a nurse and one a delivery driver, and we split everything on a spreadsheet I made. I studied accounting and spent five weeks at Pryce Audit during their busy season, ticking and tying numbers until midnight. Now I do three or four warehouse shifts through a temp agency, and I apply for audit and accounts jobs in the evenings. On a good day I also do two hours on a professional qualification book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On balance I'd say fine, maybe a little relief. I'd tell the flatmates it's the same economy with a few handy tools. I'd tell my old supervisor at Pryce that the busy season will still need warm bodies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the world stays the same, which means I have a good degree, a thin bank balance and a loan. Local audit work is tight; Pryce said they'd hire two graduates this year and had two hundred applications. I'd say my odds are about one in a hundred per application, so I need lots of applications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the numbers: thirty applications a month, with a note to Pryce each quarter so they remember me. I'd keep the warehouse shifts, enrol in the first paper of a professional accountancy qualification, because some firms pay fees for it, and use AI tools for first drafts of cover letters. I'd also keep cutting costs, like cancelling the gym.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but dull. I'm not scared, but I'm impatient. It's like a long train that keeps stopping at stations without passengers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why enrol in the qualification before you have a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because firms like it when you've already started, and a first paper costs about four hundred pounds. It's a gamble, but a small one. If I wait for a job to pay for it, I might wait a year, and by then others have passed the first exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the four hundred pounds come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From warehouse overtime and the gym I'm cancelling. It's six weeks of extra shifts, and honestly that's fine. I'd rather spend sweat than sit with an unpaid month.

say: On balance I'd say it's the **same economy** with a few handy tools.
I'd tell my old supervisor the busy season will still need **people**.
think: My odds are about **one in a hundred** per application, so I need many.
Pryce Audit had two hundred applicants for **two places**.
do: Send thirty **applications** a month and a quarterly note to Pryce.
Enrol in the first **accountancy exam** paper for four hundred pounds.
Keep the warehouse **shifts** and cancel the gym.
feel: **Steady but dull**, like a train stopping at empty stations.

Cancel the gym and review every subscription

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the numbers are on the table: fewer juniors, more software. At work I'd ask what the plan is for training. With mates I'd say it's neither doom nor salvation, just a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, audit is full of the work software handles well: matching, sampling, checking. At Pryce I saw a tool do in an hour what took me two nights. So firms need fewer juniors, and the ones they keep need to supervise the tool. I think I could be one of those, but not if I wait too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools properly now, not just for cover letters: learn the audit analytics software, and take a short data course. I'd apply to firms that talk openly about technology, and I'd keep the qualification going, because the human sign-off still needs a qualified person. I'd also keep the warehouse job going until I land something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, I guess. It's not panic, but I notice I'm checking the news more. A bit of me is curious, which surprises me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you find out which firms actually hire for the new way of working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask former interns and look at what the job ads say. If an ad lists analytics tools and an exam path, that's a sign. If it lists data entry and a six-month contract, that's the old model and it's going. I've started a spreadsheet of firms with notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to make time for the data course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekend shifts, probably, which costs about eighty pounds. And my phone games. It's a trade I'd make, as long as it pays back within a year.

At work I'd ask what the plan is for **training**.
think: Audit holds work software does well: **matching, sampling and checking**.

do: Learn the **audit analytics** software and take a short data course.
Apply to firms that talk openly about **technology**.
Keep the **qualification** going and the warehouse job.
feel: **Alert** rather than panicked, and a little curious.

steps.text: Learn an audit analytics tool through a short online course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too short for anyone to prepare, and the government needs to put up money for retraining quickly. At the warehouse I'd say little, because someone might overhear and panic. With friends I'd say let's save and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, there's no way a junior accountant survives that intact. The jobs I'm applying for are the ones to go first, and the loan stays. I'd be 25 in a world where Pryce doesn't hire graduates. I think the tax and audit work goes mostly to software by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying for the qualification, since it may be worthless, and save everything. I'd take as many warehouse shifts as the agency gives me, because robots are three years away from that. I'd also ask my parents whether I could move back to their place in Ashby for a year to cut rent, which I'd rather avoid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold, a little. Like looking at a spreadsheet where the numbers just don't add up. I'd get quiet, and my flatmates would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stop the qualification. Does that bother you after all the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a lot. It's been my plan since I was nineteen. But a plan is only good if the world matches it, and two years is a world that doesn't. I'd rather lose four hundred pounds than a thousand more on exams for a job that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when the warehouse robots come around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd hope to be in something else, maybe in a union or a public job that moves slowly. If not, I'd be in the same boat as everyone. I think the warehouse gives me three years, and I'd use every month of them.

say: I'd say two years is **too short** and government must fund retraining quickly.
With friends I'd say **save and see**.
think: No junior accountant survives that **intact**, and the loan stays.
Pryce won't hire **graduates** by the time I'm 25.
do: Stop paying for the **qualification** and save everything.
Take every **warehouse shift** the agency gives.
Ask my parents about **moving back** to Ashby for a year.
feel: **Cold**, like a spreadsheet where the numbers don't add up.
S2.quote: A plan is only good if the world matches it, and two years is a world that doesn't.
fieldNote: Abandons a plan he has held since nineteen, which is **costly** for him.
Quiet in public but tells the flatmates when asked.
Uses the warehouse as a three-year bridge before robots arrive.

steps.text: Stop paying for accountancy exam entries and save the money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast but not impossible, and people should use the time. I'd tell the flatmates to keep some savings. I'd tell the supervisor at Pryce that I'm ready to learn whatever the firm needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think five years gives me a real shot. If I qualify and land a job in the next two years, I'd have three years of experience and a pay rise before things change. The risk is the firm's role shrinks while I'm still on the junior rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the qualification, take the first audit or accounts job that lets me study, and learn the analytics tools quickly. I'd pay down the loan with every spare pound. And I'd keep looking at what the profession is saying, so I can switch sideways to risk or compliance if audit shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. It's a challenge with a clock on it, and I like those. I'd still get a quiet worry on Sunday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why risk or compliance as the sideways move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rules and sign-offs need people to be accountable, and a firm can't blame a machine in court. That's my guess, anyway. I've asked a senior from Pryce over coffee and he said the same, so it isn't only me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from the two-year scenario for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd stop everything and save. With five, I can still invest in a qualification, because it might pay off for three years before things change. It's about whether I can recover my costs in time. I'm basically doing a payback calculation.

say: I'd say five years is fast but **not impossible**.
I'd tell the flatmates to keep some **savings**.
I'd tell my old supervisor at Pryce I'm **ready to learn**.
think: Five years gives me a **real shot** if I qualify and land a job soon.
The risk is the firm's role **shrinks** while I'm still junior.
do: Push the **qualification** and take the first job that lets me study.
Pay down the **loan** with every spare pound.
feel: **Fairly steady**, a challenge with a clock, and Sunday-night worry.
S3.quote: A firm can't blame a machine in court.
fieldNote: Treats each scenario as a **payback calculation**, which shapes his choices.

steps.text: Take the first audit or accounts job that supports exam study
Pass the first two accountancy papers within the year

Pay down the loan with every spare pound

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most people will cope. I'd say there will be new jobs we can't name, as there always are. I'd tell my flatmates to stay curious and avoid panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years gives me a career. I could qualify, work for six or seven years and be comfortable. The risk is being a senior with no new skills when the change comes, so I need to keep updating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job I can, pass the qualification, and learn a new tool each year. I'd pay the loan down and save into a small pension, since compound interest loves time. I'd also help the next batch of interns, because training people is a skill the machines may not do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit boring, even, in a good way. I'd still keep a rainy-day fund because old habits stick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different about how you spend your money in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd actually spend some. A holiday, a better laptop, maybe a deposit on a flat in six years. With two years I wouldn't, but with ten I can look ahead. I'd keep a spreadsheet for it, naturally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being useful to the next set of interns look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Showing them how to tick and tie properly, how to check a number without a tool, and when to trust the software. I think there'll always be a need for somebody who understands what the tool did. I'd like to be that person.

say: I'd say there will be **new jobs** we can't name yet, as always.
I'd tell flatmates to stay **curious** and avoid panic.
think: Ten years gives me a **career**: qualify, work six or seven years, feel comfortable.
The risk is being a senior with **no new skills**.

Pay down the loan and start a small **pension**.
Help the next **interns** learn the basics.
feel: **Calm**, even a little boring, in a good way.
S4.quote: I'd pay the loan down and save into a small pension, since compound interest loves time.
fieldNote: Only the ten-year world feels **calm**, since qualifying and earning fit inside it.
Plans to spend and save, which he can't do in faster worlds.

steps.text: Take the first accounts job and pass the qualification

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my plan depends on a job and a qualification, and two years doesn't give me time for either. What would help is a way to pause the loan, firms promising graduate places, and exam fees paid by employers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that a lot of us are not panicking, we're counting. We want to know what the odds are, and then we'll do the work.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are not panicking, we're counting. We want to know what the odds are, and then we'll do the work.
portrait: Karl, 23, has a **good accounting degree**, five weeks at an audit firm and shared rented room.
He treats the search as a **numbers problem**: monthly targets, odds, exam fees and payback.
He uses AI tools **sometimes** and learns them once he sees that they work.
His mood stays anxious in most worlds because audit juniors are the **first** to be replaced.
Only ten years lets him feel **calm**, with time to qualify and save.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, because his plan needs a job and an exam, and two years allows neither.
whatWouldHelp: A way to pause the **loan**, firms promising graduate places, and employers paying **exam fees**.
